keywords: Screw screwdriver wrench spanner cochlea cōchlea vertitōrium clāvis mēchanica screw driver Neo-Latin technical variable quantity powered drill driver

items.html: cōchlea / cochlea, -ae f. — screw. Ancient cochlea already denotes spiral and screw mechanisms; later technical Latin applies it directly to the modern threaded fastener.
Lewis & Short marks the first vowel of cochlea as variable (cō̆-), so this lexicon does not pretend that one quantity is uniquely correct.
vertitōrium, -ī n. — screwdriver [Neo-Latin lexicographic term; Helfer]. Morgan–Owens also records the descriptive īnstrūmentum cochleīs extorquendīs from Latham.
clāvis mēchanica — wrench / spanner [Neo-Latin lexicographic term]. clāvis Anglica is also recorded for a universal/adjustable wrench.

Modern Latin sources do not maintain a single universally standardized terminology for every modern screwdriver, screw and wrench subtype; specific types should therefore be formed or selected case by case.
Cochleam vertitōriō intorque. — Screw the screw in with the screwdriver. Clāvem mēchanicam affer. — Bring the wrench.
vertitōrium ēlectricum — powered screwdriver / drill-driver. Our descriptive qualification of the recorded noun; a drill-driver also drills, which a hand screwdriver cannot.

keywords: Nut bolt screw thread mātrix cochleae cochlea fēmina rūgae intorquēre firmāre retorquēre Neo-Latin lexicographic evidence

items.html: mātrix cochleae — nut used with a bolt or screw; Morgan–Owens cites Scheller’s 1783 lexicon. cochlea fēmina is another recorded expression.
rūgae f. pl. — screw threads in later technical lexicography. The connection is old: Pliny uses singular rūga for a female screw.
cochleam intorquēre — turn/screw a screw in [18th-century evidence].
firmāre cochleā — fasten or tighten with a screw [19th-century / Helfer].
cochleam retorquēre — unscrew; cochleam evolvere is another recorded expression.

The modern English distinction between screw and bolt is not mapped consistently onto one fixed pair of Latin nouns in the sources checked. cochlea is therefore kept broad here rather than creating a false precision.

keywords: Dowel wall plug wall anchor expansion plug scalmus ancora mūrālis plastica working formation Neo-Latin extension

items.html: scalmus, scalmī m. — ancient peg or thole-pin; Morgan–Owens/Helfer extends it to an English dowel, i.e. a solid joining pin.

A dowel is not the plastic insert for a screw in a wall. That object is usually a wall plug, wall anchor or expansion plug: an insert placed in a drilled hole so that a screw can grip masonry or another material.

ancora mūrālis plastica — plastic wall anchor / wall plug [our provisional descriptive formation]. It is intentionally labelled rather than presented as an established Neo-Latin dictionary term; no securely established exact equivalent was found in the Latin sources checked.
Ancoram mūrālem plasticam in forāmen pōne. — Put the plastic wall plug into the hole.

english: Adze / hew / dress timber / box of nails
keywords: Adze / hew / dress timber ascia, asciae f.; dolō, dolāre Ancient Latin ascia, asciae f. — adze, the carpenter’s axe for dressing timber. Lewis & Short: “an axe for hewing wood, a carpenter’s axe”; secūris is the ordinary axe. Pliny, NH 7.198 makes Daedalus the inventor of carpentry and of its first tools: fabricam māteriāriam Daedalus et in eā serram, asciam, perpendiculum, terebram . The square and the level go to Theodorus of Samos (see plane / square ). Pliny, NH 16.207: lime wood blunts adzes fastest, mollissima tilia … quod citissimē asciās retundat . Vitruvius 7.2.2: the adze also tests slaked lime, sūmātur ascia et, quemadmodum māteria dolātur, sīc calx in lacū mācerāta asciētur ; if the lime clings to the iron like glue, it is ready for plastering. dolō, dolāre, dolāvī, dolātum — hew, chip into shape with an axe or adze. Cato, Agr. 14 dolābit, secābit , of the contractor’s timber work; Cicero, Div. 2.86 (Lewis & Short). Asciam mihi dā. — Give me the adze. Faber tignum asciā dolat. — The carpenter is dressing the beam with the adze. Composed examples. capsa clāvōrum — box of nails; pulsō, pulsāre — strike, knock. For the plane and square, the trowel and the plumb line see their own entries; hammer, saw, nails and chisel are in the basic tool entry. malleus, serra, ascia, quam Bulgarī teslam vocant, secūris, terebra, scalprum, rēgula, norma, forceps, runcīna, trulla, quā tēctōrēs tēctōrium indūcunt, līnea cum perpendiculō, capsa clāvōrum — hammer, saw, the adze the Bulgarians call tesla, axe, drill, chisel, ruler, square, pincers, plane, the trowel plasterers spread plaster with, a plumb line, a box of nails (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae ). quī trabem asciā dolābat — who was dressing a beam with the adze (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae ). «Asciam nōvī!» inquit Theodōrus. «Asciam volō!» — I know the adze! I want the adze! (Fābula VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae ). Dā mihi, ōrō, ūtendum malleum, tata! — Lend me the hammer, please, Dad! (after Pont. Progymn. english: Hook / hook onto / catch with a hook
latin: uncus, uncī m.; hāmus, hāmī m.
keywords: Hook / hook onto / catch with a hook uncus, uncī m.; hāmus, hāmī m. Ancient words Composed descriptions uncus, uncī m. — general hook. hāmus, hāmī m. — hook, especially a fishhook. Traupman gives a clothes hook as uncus vestiārius (p. 123) and a fishhook as hāmus (p. 47). prehendō, prehendere — catch or take hold of; uncō prehendere — catch with a hook, our descriptive phrase. affīgō, affīgere, affīxī, affīxum — fasten or attach; uncō affīgere — fasten with a hook, our descriptive phrase. uncō can also be the dative “to a hook”; the construction and context determine the relation. Hoc huic uncō affīge. — Hook this onto this hook / attach this to this hook. Uncum affer. — Bring the hook. aduncus, adunca, aduncum — hook-shaped / hooked. bacillum aduncum — a hooked stick; our reader series uses the diminutive bacillum for Theo’s stick. Livy 1.18.7 has baculum sine nōdō aduncum , but there it is the augur’s crook, the lituus , not an ordinary stick. A stick can have a hooked end without being a purpose-made hook. suspendō, suspendere — hang up / suspend. Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit. — Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. Our composed example for hooking the stick over a scaffolding bar and leaving it hanging. trānsversārium is Vitruvius’s crosspiece (see the scaffold-members entry ); a scaffold tube is not a vectis (lever, crowbar). For suspendere ex + ablative compare Vergil, G. 2.389 oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnū . Bacillō aduncō trānsversārium prehendit. — He caught / hooked the crossbar with the hooked stick. Our composed example when he keeps holding the stick and catches the bar with its curved end. affīgere emphasizes attachment or fastening; it is not a universal equivalent of English “hook.” uncus need not name a separately manufactured item, but describing this whole object as a bacillum aduncum is clearer. Choose the verb according to the action and result. The two English verb senses are expressed compositionally; neither phrase is presented as a separately verified technical headword. Hoc huic uncō affīge. — Hook this onto this hook / attach this to this hook. Uncum affer. — Bring the hook.

aduncus, adunca, aduncum — hook-shaped / hooked. bacillum aduncum — a hooked stick; our reader series uses the diminutive bacillum for Theo’s stick. Livy 1.18.7 has baculum sine nōdō aduncum, but there it is the augur’s crook, the lituus, not an ordinary stick. A stick can have a hooked end without being a purpose-made hook.

suspendō, suspendere — hang up / suspend. Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit. — Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. Our composed example for hooking the stick over a scaffolding bar and leaving it hanging. trānsversārium is Vitruvius’s crosspiece (see the scaffold-members entry); a scaffold tube is not a vectis (lever, crowbar). For suspendere ex + ablative compare Vergil, G. 2.389 oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnū.
Bacillō aduncō trānsversārium prehendit. — He caught / hooked the crossbar with the hooked stick. Our composed example when he keeps holding the stick and catches the bar with its curved end.

affīgere emphasizes attachment or fastening; it is not a universal equivalent of English “hook.” uncus need not name a separately manufactured item, but describing this whole object as a bacillum aduncum is clearer. Choose the verb according to the action and result.

blocks.html: The two English verb senses are expressed compositionally; neither phrase is presented as a separately verified technical headword.

keywords: Pipe / water pipe / tube fistula, fistulae f.; tubulus, tubulī m. fistula, fistulae f. — pipe or tube. fistula aquāria; fistulae aquāriae f. — water pipe; recorded in Morgan–Owens and Traupman (p. 124). tubulus, tubulī m. — small pipe or tube; Morgan–Owens also records it for plumbing. Fistulam aquāriam affer. — Bring the water pipe. Aqua per fistulam fluit. — Water flows through the pipe. Classical plumbing: Vitruvius 8.6.1 fistulīs plumbeīs seu tubulīs fictilibus — lead pipes or clay tubes; Varro, LL 5.123 fistula, ā quā fūsus aquae . These are the construction/plumbing senses; English “pipe” as a smoking implement or musical instrument needs its own context.
